title: draft-atwood-mimi-keepalive: the keepalive MIMI will need (ha ha only serious)
description:
Mark, 2026-11-27: 'bead out a ha ha only serious ping pong and keepalive id for mimi', after 'i know the ietf hates pingpong, until reality intrudes' and 'yeah, yell that SHOULD NOT louder, im sure they will listen'.

WHAT IS MISSING. MIMI defines no liveness primitive. Checked 2026-11-27 in ~/PROJECT/IETF/specs: draft-ietf-mimi-protocol-07, draft-ietf-mimi-content-10, draft-ietf-mimi-arch-03, draft-ietf-mimi-room-policy-04 and draft-ietf-mls-extensions-11 contain no ping, pong, keepalive, heartbeat or liveness, in any case. Request/response over HTTPS needs none; a long-lived carrier for delivery does, and MIMI leaves that to each binding, which means each implementation invents its own constants. mimid has four invented ones already (two 90 s keepalive times in the IRC front end, a 10..3600 s clamp on push pings at both ends, and a read timeout derived from the far end's ping interval).

THE HA HA. The IETF concedes keepalives one protocol at a time, always after deployment forces it: TCP's is a MAY with a warning not to use it (RFC 1122 4.2.3.6), HTTP/2 took PING (RFC 9113 6.7), QUIC took PING and PATH_CHALLENGE (RFC 9000 19.2, 19.17), WebSocket took Ping/Pong because middleboxes reap idle sockets (RFC 6455 5.5.2), DNS took edns-tcp-keepalive (RFC 7828), SIP took outbound keepalives (RFC 5626 3.5), ICE took consent freshness (RFC 7675). RFC 5382 asked middleboxes for 2 h 4 min of TCP idle; the field settled on about 60 s. A SHOULD NOT aimed at a load balancer is not an interoperability mechanism.

THE SERIOUS PART, what the I-D should say.
1. The keepalive is a MIMI-layer request and response, not a transport frame. Its answer MUST be produced by the component that answers ordinary requests, so that it asserts something: this provider can serve this room now. A pong emitted by a socket layer, a proxy or a timer task asserts only that the socket layer is turning, which is the failure this exists to detect.
2. The interval is negotiated, not invented: the provider states the longest idle it will tolerate and the shortest probe it will answer, and the client picks inside that. No constant per implementation.
3. Say what the answer does not assert: nothing about a remote provider, nothing about delivery already accepted, nothing about a room the asker is not in.
4. It costs what a cheap request costs: same credential as any request, rate limited per sender, and never a way for an unauthenticated peer to make a provider work. An unauthenticated or pre-authentication connection gets at most a transport-level answer.
5. No new oracle: the answer is identical whether or not the named room exists and whether or not the asker is a member, or the probe takes no room at all.
6. Revalidate an idle carrier before trusting it to carry delivery again, as ICE consent freshness does, rather than discovering it is dead on the next real request.

FOR MIMID. Adopting it would replace the invented constants and let the front ends share one mechanism; the live stream binding has no keepalive of any kind today (see the bead for that), so it is the first consumer.

NEVER MENTION JMAP in anything sent to the MIMI working group (AGENTS.md): the I-D is framed on MIMI's own transport abstraction, and the carrier that motivates it is described as a long-lived delivery carrier, nothing more.

NOT SENT. Needs Mark's OK, like any upstream post, and probably a WG issue first rather than an I-D.

NOT SENT. This is the draft text for draft-atwood-mimi-keepalive-00,
held here for Mark to read and decide. Nothing has been posted to the
MIMI working group or submitted to the datatracker. Boilerplate
(Status of This Memo, Copyright Notice, Table of Contents) is
generated and is not reproduced here. The design choices Mark settled
on 2026-11-27 are recorded in Appendix B with their reasons; one
question is still open there.


More Instant Messaging Interoperability                       M. Atwood
Internet-Draft                                       Review Commit, LLC
Intended status: Standards Track                       27 November 2026
Expires: 31 May 2027


                          A Keepalive for MIMI
                     draft-atwood-mimi-keepalive-00

Abstract

   More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) defines no way for
   one party to ask another whether it is still able to serve
   requests.  Over request/response HTTPS none is needed.  Where a
   long-lived carrier delivers room events and messages, one is
   needed, and MIMI leaves it to each carrier, so each
   implementation invents its own probe and its own timers.

   This document defines a keepalive exchange in MIMI's own framing:
   a request carrying a fresh nonce and a response that the
   component answering ordinary requests produces.  The responder
   states the longest idle it tolerates and the shortest probe it
   answers, and the prober chooses inside that range, so no
   implementation needs a constant of its own.  The probe names
   nothing.  The document states what a successful response does not
   assert, requires the same credential and rate limiting as any
   other request, and requires an idle carrier to be revalidated
   before it carries delivery again.

1.  Introduction

1.1.  What MIMI Defines Today

   MIMI server-to-server traffic is HTTPS request/response over
   mutually authenticated TLS (Section 4.1 of
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol]).  A request either gets a response or
   it does not, and the HTTP status code is the liveness signal.
   Nothing more is required.

   The MIMI documents define no liveness primitive of any kind.
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol], [I-D.ietf-mimi-content],
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-arch] and [I-D.ietf-mimi-room-policy] contain no
   ping, no pong, no keepalive, no heartbeat and no liveness
   mechanism.

   A carrier that outlives a single request/response pair changes
   that.  Its two ends are two implementations, and they have to
   agree on two things no document states: what an answer to a probe
   means, and how often a probe may be sent and will be answered.
   This document states both, so that two implementations can match
   rather than each choosing.

1.2.  Why Implementations Invent Constants

   A carrier that stays open while idle is reaped by whatever sits
   in the path.  [RFC5382] asked a NAT for an established-connection
   idle timeout of no less than 2 hours 4 minutes (REQ-5, Section 5
   of [RFC5382]); deployed middleboxes and load balancers reap an
   idle connection in about a minute.  An implementation that wants
   its carrier to survive therefore probes, and because no document
   tells it how often, it picks a number.

   One implementation, mimid, has four such numbers, each marked in
   its source as invented and not from any specification:

   *  90 seconds of silence before its IRC front end probes a
      client, and 90 seconds for the client to answer.

   *  30 seconds of silence before either end of a second, binary
      delivery carrier between a client and its provider sends a
      transport-level probe, chosen below 60 seconds because that is
      where deployed middleboxes reap an idle connection.

   *  75 seconds, twice the far end's stated interval plus 15
      seconds, the read timeout the reader of a long-lived push
      stream derives for itself.

   *  10 seconds to 3600 seconds, the range to which a provider
      clamps a probe interval a client asks for on the stream it
      offers.

   Two implementations that each pick in good faith produce a
   carrier that one end believes is alive and the other has closed.
   The cost is not theoretical: in that implementation a probe is
   answered only once the component that answers ordinary requests
   is free to answer it, so a client whose timeout is shorter than a
   long synchronization gives up during one.  Which timeout is right
   depends on what the other end does, and no document says.

1.3.  Precedent

   The IETF has conceded a keepalive to one protocol at a time,
   each time after deployment forced it:

   *  TCP's keepalive is a MAY, carrying a warning against relying
      on it, defaulting to off, with an interval defaulting to no
      less than two hours (Section 4.2.3.6 of [RFC1122]).

   *  HTTP/2 has PING, for round-trip time and for "determining
      whether an idle connection is still functional", echoed with
      identical payload (Section 6.7 of [RFC9113]).

   *  QUIC has PING (Section 19.2 of [RFC9000]) and PATH_CHALLENGE
      (Section 19.17 of [RFC9000]).

   *  WebSocket has Ping and Pong (Section 5.5.2 of [RFC6455]).

   *  DNS over TCP has edns-tcp-keepalive, by which a server signals
      a variable idle timeout rather than letting each client guess
      [RFC7828].

   *  SIP outbound has a keepalive technique for its flows
      (Section 3.5 of [RFC5626]).

   *  ICE has consent freshness: consent expires after 30 seconds,
      an endpoint must cease transmission when it does, and must
      regain consent before resuming (Section 5.1 of [RFC7675]).

   Every one of these is a liveness primitive the protocol was
   designed without.  MIMI is now at the point where one of its
   carriers stays open.

1.4.  What This Document Does

   This document defines a keepalive request and response in MIMI's
   framing, usable on any carrier that carries MIMI protocol
   messages, with:

   *  a rule about which component produces the answer, so that the
      answer asserts something (Section 4.2);

   *  a negotiated interval, replacing the per-implementation
      constant (Section 4.3);

   *  a statement of what the answer does not assert (Section 5);

   *  the cost and authorization rules of an ordinary request
      (Section 6);

   *  a probe that names nothing and an answer derived from no
      per-room state (Section 7);

   *  revalidation of an idle carrier before it carries delivery
      again (Section 4.5).

   It does not define a carrier, and it does not replace the
   transport's own keepalive (Section 8).

2.  Conventions and Definitions

   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL
   NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED",
   "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as
   described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they
   appear in all capitals, as shown here.

   Carrier:  a connection, stream or association over which MIMI
      protocol messages are exchanged and which outlives a single
      request/response pair.  A carrier may run between two
      providers or between a client and its own provider.

   Prober:  the party that sends a KeepAliveRequest.

   Responder:  the party that receives it.

   Serving component:  the component of the responder that produces
      responses to the MIMI endpoints of Section 5 of
      [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol].  Not a TLS terminator, reverse
      proxy, load balancer, connection multiplexer or timer task.

   Idle:  a carrier is idle for as long as no MIMI protocol message
      has been received on it.

3.  Overview

   A prober sends a KeepAliveRequest carrying a fresh nonce.  The
   responder's serving component reads it and returns a
   KeepAliveResponse echoing that nonce, together with the longest
   idle the responder tolerates on the carrier and the shortest
   interval at which it will answer a probe.  The prober probes at
   an interval inside that range.  While successful responses keep
   arriving, both ends may use the carrier for delivery.  When they
   stop, the prober stops sending delivery traffic on the carrier
   and must obtain a successful response before resuming.

   A successful response asserts exactly one thing: the serving
   component reachable on this carrier read this probe and answered
   it.  Section 5 lists what it does not assert.

4.  The Keepalive Exchange

4.1.  Messages

   The structures below use the TLS presentation language (Section 3
   of [RFC8446]), as the rest of MIMI does, and are carried with the
   media type application/mimi-protocol (Section 10.6 of
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol]).

   struct {
       Protocol protocol;
       opaque nonce<V>;
   } KeepAliveRequest;

   enum {
       ok(0),
       unavailable(1),
       tooFrequent(2),
       (255)
   } KeepAliveStatus;

   struct {
       opaque nonce<V>;
       KeepAliveStatus status;
       uint32 maxIdleSeconds;
       uint32 minIntervalSeconds;
   } KeepAliveResponse;

   The request carries no room identifier and no other selector.  A
   responder MUST NOT define one, and MUST NOT vary a response by
   anything the prober supplies beyond the nonce.  The exchange is
   about the carrier and the component answering on it, and nothing
   else; see Section 7.

   The nonce MUST be at least 8 and at most 64 octets, MUST be freshly
   generated for each probe from a cryptographically secure source, and
   MUST NOT be reused on a carrier.  The responder MUST copy it into the
   response unchanged.  A prober MUST discard a response whose nonce
   does not match an outstanding probe of its own, and MUST NOT
   count such a response as a successful probe.

   maxIdleSeconds is the longest the responder will leave the carrier
   open while idle.  minIntervalSeconds is the shortest interval between
   probes the responder undertakes to answer.  A responder MUST set both
   to non-zero values in every KeepAliveResponse it sends, and MUST
   leave room for two probes and their answers in one idle period by
   setting 3 x minIntervalSeconds to less than maxIdleSeconds.

   That figure is derived rather than chosen, which is why it is the
   only number this document states.  Section 4.4 requires two
   unanswered probes before a carrier is declared dead and Section 4.3
   allows each to be paced at up to 1.2 times the period the prober
   chose, which accounts for 2.4; the remaining 0.6 of a period is the
   budget for the second answer to arrive, so that arithmetic cannot
   call a carrier alive while it is being reaped.

4.2.  Which Component Answers

   A response with status ok MUST be produced by the serving
   component, after that component has read the probe, and MUST NOT
   be produced by any other part of the responder.  In particular it
   MUST NOT be produced by a TLS terminator, a reverse proxy, a load
   balancer, a connection multiplexer, a timer task, or from a
   precomputed or cached buffer.

   A responder whose serving component cannot currently serve ordinary
   requests on the carrier MUST NOT send status ok.  It MUST either send
   status unavailable or send nothing.

   Status unavailable MAY be produced without reaching the serving
   component, as status tooFrequent may (Section 4.3).  A responder
   whose serving component is blocked has nothing else that could
   produce it, so the restriction above applies to status ok alone.  A
   prober MUST therefore read status unavailable as a courtesy and never
   as evidence about the responder: it is not an answer to the probe,
   and Section 4.5 applies to a carrier that has received only
   unavailable exactly as it applies to a silent one.

   A responder MUST NOT answer a probe before its serving component
   is able to answer it.  Deferring the answer until then is the
   mechanism: an answer emitted while the serving component is
   blocked would report that the socket layer is turning, which is
   the failure this exchange exists to detect.

   A responder that partitions rooms across instances asserts the
   liveness of the instance the carrier reaches, and of no other.
   This document defines no way to ask about a particular room; see
   Appendix B.

   A prober MUST NOT treat status unavailable as a successful probe.
   A prober MAY continue to probe after receiving it, subject to
   Section 4.3, and MUST apply Section 4.5 before resuming delivery
   traffic.

4.3.  Negotiating the Interval

   A binding MUST convey the responder's maxIdleSeconds and
   minIntervalSeconds to the prober when the carrier is established, as
   a DNS server signals its idle timeout rather than letting each client
   guess [RFC7828].  Where there is no carrier establishment to carry
   them, as in request/response HTTPS, the responder MUST publish both
   values wherever the prober learns the endpoint; Section 9 puts them
   in the directory document.  A prober MUST hold both values, from one
   of those two places, before its first probe.

   A responder MUST restate both values in every KeepAliveResponse it
   sends, and those values supersede any earlier ones for the remainder
   of the carrier.

   A prober that has no values for a carrier MUST NOT send a probe: it
   has no pacing it can be sure the responder will answer.  A prober
   MUST NOT assume a default for either value.  This document states no
   default and no recommended period, because a default is how one
   codebase arrives at four invented constants.

   A prober MUST choose a base period P with minIntervalSeconds <= P and
   with 3 x P less than maxIdleSeconds, so that two probes and their
   answers fall inside one idle period.  It MUST derive each interval by
   randomizing P between 0.8 and 1.2 times its value, so that probes
   from many probers do not synchronize.  This is the pacing rule of
   Section 5.1 of [RFC7675].

   A responder that changes either value MUST answer one further probe
   paced by the previous values, and MUST NOT close the carrier for
   idleness sooner than the previous maxIdleSeconds allowed, so that a
   prober pacing itself by what it was last told is neither refused nor
   reaped.

   A responder MAY answer a probe that arrives sooner than
   minIntervalSeconds after the previous one with status tooFrequent.
   Producing that response MUST NOT cost the responder more than
   producing status ok, and it MAY be produced without reaching the
   serving component.  A prober that receives it MUST NOT count the
   probe as successful, and MUST wait at least minIntervalSeconds from
   its previous probe before sending the next one.

4.4.  Failure

   A prober MUST NOT declare a carrier dead on a single unanswered
   probe.  The caution of Section 4.2.3.6 of [RFC1122] applies here
   too: one lost probe or one lost answer is an ordinary event.  A
   prober MUST send at least two probes, unanswered, before
   declaring the carrier dead.

   A prober MUST declare the carrier dead once no response with status
   ok has been received on it within maxIdleSeconds, and MUST then stop
   sending delivery traffic on it, as an ICE endpoint ceases
   transmission when consent expires (Section 5.1 of [RFC7675]).

   A responder MAY close a carrier that has been idle longer than
   maxIdleSeconds.

   A carrier's death is not delivery.  Events and messages sent on a
   carrier that is declared dead, and not acknowledged by the mechanism
   that ordinarily acknowledges them, MUST be retained for redelivery.

4.5.  Revalidating an Idle Carrier

   A prober that has not received a response with status ok on a carrier
   within the last maxIdleSeconds MUST obtain one before sending any
   further delivery traffic on that carrier.  This mirrors the
   requirement of Section 5.1 of [RFC7675] to regain consent before
   resuming.

   A prober SHOULD revalidate a carrier it has held idle before it
   has traffic to send, rather than discovering the carrier is dead
   from the failure of the next real request.

5.  What a Successful Response Does Not Assert

   A response with status ok asserts that the serving component
   reachable on this carrier read the probe and answered it.  It
   asserts nothing else.  In particular:

   *  It MUST NOT be taken as an assertion about any other provider.
      A follower's probe answered by a hub says nothing about the
      hub's reachability to other followers, and a hub's probe
      answered by a follower says nothing about that follower's
      clients.

   *  It MUST NOT be taken as an acknowledgement of any event or
      message previously accepted on the carrier, nor as evidence
      that such an event has been fanned out, stored, or made
      available to any client.  Delivery is acknowledged by the
      mechanisms that acknowledge delivery, not by this exchange.

   *  It MUST NOT be taken as an assertion about the state,
      existence, policy or membership of any room.  The probe names
      no room and the answer reports on none.

   *  It MUST NOT be taken as an assertion that a subsequent request
      will succeed, or that the prober is authorized to make one.

   An implementation MUST NOT make the success of a request
   conditional on a prior successful probe, other than as required
   by Section 4.5.

6.  Cost and Authorization

   A KeepAliveRequest is a request.  It MUST be authorized exactly
   as any other request on the same carrier is authorized, by the
   same credential and at the same boundary, and MUST be rejected
   where an ordinary request would be rejected.  Where MIMI
   server-to-server authentication applies (Section 4.1 of
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol]), a probe MUST be authenticated the same
   way.

   A responder MUST NOT process a KeepAliveRequest received on a
   carrier that is not yet authenticated, and MUST NOT send any
   KeepAliveResponse on such a carrier.  A party that wants liveness
   before authentication completes has the transport's own keepalive
   (Section 8) and nothing more at the MIMI layer.  This exchange
   MUST NOT become a way for an unauthenticated peer to make a
   responder do work.

   A responder MUST rate limit probes per authenticated sender, not
   per carrier and not per source address, so that opening further
   carriers does not buy further probes.  A responder MUST limit the
   work a probe can cost to that of the cheapest ordinary request it
   serves; a probe MUST NOT cause a read of room state, a policy
   evaluation, a cryptographic operation on room material, or a
   request to another provider.

   A responder MAY count probes toward whatever request budget it
   applies to the sender.

7.  Carrying No Selector

   A KeepAliveRequest carries a nonce and nothing else, so there is
   nothing in it for a response to depend on.  Every response on a
   carrier MUST be identical in every octet except the echoed nonce
   and, where they have changed, the two interval values.  A
   responder MUST NOT derive any part of a response from room state,
   from the prober's membership of any room, or from any other state
   that an unauthorized prober could not already read.

   A responder MUST NOT vary its timing in answering a probe by any
   such state, and SHOULD produce the response without consulting
   per-room state at all, which is the simplest way to satisfy this.

   A field that must not affect an answer is a field that eventually
   affects somebody's answer, and that implementation becomes the
   oracle this section exists to forbid.  A per-room probe is
   therefore not defined here rather than defined and then
   restricted; see Appendix B.

8.  Relationship to Transport Keepalives

   A carrier may have a keepalive of its own: HTTP/2 PING
   (Section 6.7 of [RFC9113]), WebSocket Ping (Section 5.5.2 of
   [RFC6455]), QUIC PING (Section 19.2 of [RFC9000]), TCP keepalive
   (Section 4.2.3.6 of [RFC1122]).

   Those mechanisms remain useful and this document does not replace
   them.  They maintain path state and detect a broken path, and
   they are available before the carrier is authenticated.  An
   implementation SHOULD continue to use the transport's keepalive
   for path maintenance.

   A transport-level answer MUST NOT be taken as an answer to a
   KeepAliveRequest, and a responder MUST NOT answer a
   KeepAliveRequest with a transport-level frame.  A transport
   keepalive is answered by the component that owns the connection,
   which is the component whose liveness is not in question.

9.  Binding Considerations

   A binding that carries MIMI protocol messages over a carrier MUST
   state how a KeepAliveRequest and a KeepAliveResponse are framed on
   it, and MUST convey the responder's two interval values when the
   carrier is established (Section 4.3).  A binding that cannot carry
   two integers at carrier establishment cannot implement this
   document.

   Where MIMI server-to-server traffic is request/response HTTPS, as
   in [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol], no keepalive is needed and an
   implementation SHOULD NOT send one: a request that gets a
   response has already proved what a probe would prove.  For that
   case this document defines a directory entry only, so that a
   deployment holding connections open across requests has one
   mechanism available rather than a per-implementation invention:

   "keepAlive": {
       "uri": "https://mimi.example.com/v1/keepAlive",
       "maxIdleSeconds": 240,
       "minIntervalSeconds": 60
   }

   A provider that supports this exchange over HTTPS MUST include that
   entry in its directory document (Section 5.1 of
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol]) with all three members, MUST accept a POST
   of a KeepAliveRequest to that URI, and MUST return a
   KeepAliveResponse with HTTP status 200 for every status value of
   Section 4.1, so that the HTTP status code carries no information the
   body does not (Section 7).

   The two values belong in the entry because there is no carrier
   establishment here to carry them and a prober holding neither may
   send nothing (Section 4.3).  Those shown are the example provider's
   own; this document recommends no values and states none.

10.  Security Considerations

   The exchange is an authenticated request that does no work, and
   its risks are those of such a request.

   Amplification and work:  Section 6 requires the same credential
      as any other request, a per-sender rate limit, and a work
      bound.  Without those a probe is a cheap way to make a
      responder expensive, and a carrier is a cheap way to multiply
      it.

   Disclosure:  a probe carries a nonce and nothing else, and
      Section 7 forbids an answer derived from room state, so the
      exchange is not a way to learn whether a room exists or who is
      in it.  An implementation that accepted a room identifier and
      answered "unavailable" for an unknown room and "ok" for a
      known one would have built the oracle this document forbids,
      which is why the field is absent rather than ignored.

   False confidence:  a liveness mechanism is dangerous in
      proportion to what its users read into it.  Section 5 states
      the limits, and the rule in Section 4.2 about which component
      answers exists so that a successful probe asserts something
      beyond the health of a socket.

   Spoofed answers:  the nonce requirement of Section 4.1 keeps an
      answer from being replayed or precomputed.  It does not
      authenticate the responder; that is the carrier's job, and on
      an unauthenticated carrier this exchange is not used at all
      (Section 6).

   Idle carriers:  a carrier held open and unvalidated is a carrier
      whose far end may be gone.  Section 4.5 requires revalidation
      before delivery resumes, so that the loss is found by a probe
      rather than by a message.

11.  IANA Considerations

   This document defines no new media type; a KeepAliveRequest and
   KeepAliveResponse are carried with application/mimi-protocol
   (Section 10.6 of [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol]).

   This document defines the directory document key "keepAlive"
   (Section 9), whose value is an object carrying the endpoint URI and
   the responder's two interval values.
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol] establishes no registry for directory
   document keys, so no registration is requested here.  If such a
   registry is created, this key belongs in it.

   If the MIMI working group folds this mechanism into
   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol], the structures of Section 4.1 and the
   directory key belong there and this document should not be
   published separately.

12.1.  Normative References

   [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol]  Barnes, R. L., Hodgson, M., Kohbrok,
              K., Mahy, R., Ralston, T., and R. Robert, "More

              and MLS", Work in Progress, Internet-Draft,
              draft-ietf-mimi-protocol-07, 2 November 2026.

   [RFC2119]  Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate
              Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119,
              DOI 10.17487/RFC2119, March 1997.

   [RFC7675]  Perumal, M., Wing, D., Ravindranath, R., Reddy, T.,
              and M. Thomson, "Session Traversal Utilities for NAT
              (STUN) Usage for Consent Freshness", RFC 7675,
              DOI 10.17487/RFC7675, October 2015.

   [RFC8174]  Leiba, B., "Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC
              2119 Key Words", BCP 14, RFC 8174,
              DOI 10.17487/RFC8174, May 2017.

   [RFC8446]  Rescorla, E., "The Transport Layer Security (TLS)
              Protocol Version 1.3", RFC 8446,
              DOI 10.17487/RFC8446, August 2018.

12.2.  Informative References

   [I-D.ietf-mimi-arch]  Barnes, R. L., "An Architecture for More

Appendix A.  Implementation Experience

   The constants of Section 1.2 are from mimid, an open-source
   implementation of MIMI over MLS.  Each is marked in its source as
   invented and not derived from any specification, which is the point:
   there was nothing to derive them from.  Adopting this exchange would
   replace all four with a negotiated pair of values and let that
   implementation's several front ends share one mechanism.

   The rule of Section 4.2 is from that implementation's experience and
   not from reasoning alone.  Its IRC front end answered a client's
   probe from the task that owned the connection, which could answer
   while the component that serves ordinary requests was held for
   minutes by an unrelated operation.  The probe reported a healthy
   socket throughout, and the client learned otherwise only when a real
   request of its own timed out.  Moving the answer behind that
   component made the probe report the condition the client was asking
   about, and made one stall visible as a missing answer rather than as
   a slow message.  A keepalive that cannot do that is a keepalive that
   confirms the wrong thing.

   No claim of conformance to this document, or to any MIMI document, is
   made for that implementation here.

Appendix B.  Design Choices and Open Issues

   Five choices were settled while this document was drafted.  They
   are recorded with their reasons, because each is a place where a
   reader would otherwise ask why the obvious thing was not done.

   *  The two interval values reach the prober before its first
      probe, and no default or recommended period appears anywhere in
      this document.  A default is how one codebase arrives at four
      invented constants.  A binding that cannot carry two integers
      at carrier establishment cannot implement this document, which
      is a deliberate floor rather than an oversight; a transport
      with no establishment at all publishes them beside the endpoint
      instead, which is what Section 9 does for request/response
      HTTPS.  Requiring establishment alone would have left that
      endpoint advertisable and unusable, since a prober with no
      values may not probe.

   *  The pacing floor is 3 x minIntervalSeconds < maxIdleSeconds,
      so that two probes and their answers fit inside one idle
      period with room for the jitter Section 4.3 requires.  It
      forbids a responder from advertising a pair of values no
      prober could satisfy.  An earlier draft used 2.4, which is
      the two probes alone; it left no budget for the second answer
      to arrive, so a slow path satisfied the arithmetic while the
      carrier was being reaped.

   *  Status unavailable stays, although silence carries the same
      information with one fewer code path.  A responder that is
      reachable but cannot serve is exactly the condition this
      document exists to report, and reporting it is cheaper for the
      prober than waiting out a timeout.  It is worth less than
      status ok and Section 4.2 says so: a blocked serving component
      cannot produce it, so something else does, which is why it
      counts as a courtesy and not as an answer.

   *  The probe carries no room identifier.  An earlier design
      carried one so that a responder partitioning rooms across
      instances could route the probe, and then forbade the answer
      from depending on it.  Carrying a field that must not affect
      the answer means every implementation ignoring it correctly
      and one implementation eventually not, and that one becomes
      the oracle Section 7 forbids.  Per-room liveness can be added
      later with the indistinguishability rule designed in, which is
      not possible once a field exists and is merely restricted.

   *  Intended status is Standards Track.  The mechanism is one two
      implementations have to agree on exactly, which is what the
      track is for.

   One issue is open:

   *  Whether this belongs in [I-D.ietf-mimi-protocol] rather than in
      a document of its own.  The structures are small and the
      directory already has a place for the endpoint.  Section 11
      says what should happen to this document if the working group
      folds the mechanism in.

2026-11-27, three fixes to the rewritten draft, found reading it back with Mark. Still NOT SENT.

1. THE HTTPS ENDPOINT WAS ADVERTISABLE AND UNUSABLE. §4.3 said the two interval values reach the prober when the carrier is established and that a prober holding neither MUST NOT probe; §9's directory entry was a bare URI, and request/response HTTPS has no establishment. So a provider could publish `keepAlive` and no conforming prober could ever use it. The entry is now an object carrying `uri`, `maxIdleSeconds` and `minIntervalSeconds`, all three required, and §4.3 names publication beside the endpoint as the second of exactly two places the values may come from. §11 says the key's value is that object. The example reads 240 and 60, which satisfies the document's own floor, and says the values are the example provider's rather than a recommendation.

This was not one of Mark's five decisions; it was introduced by combining decision 5's no-default rule with the directory entry the first version already had.

2. THE PACING FLOOR IS 3, NOT 2.4. Two probes paced at up to 1.2 x P account for 2.4; the second answer still had to arrive inside the same idle period and nothing reserved time for it, so a slow path satisfied the arithmetic while the carrier was being reaped. The remaining 0.6 of a period is now that budget. §4.1 states the figure as derived rather than chosen, and says it is the only number the document states, which is the objection a reviewer reaches for first. Appendix B records 2.4 and why it was wrong.

3. WHO MAY PRODUCE `unavailable`. §4.2 forbids anything but the serving component from producing `ok`, and a responder whose serving component is blocked has nothing else that could produce `unavailable` either. The restriction therefore applies to `ok` alone, which the section now says, with the consequence: a prober reads `unavailable` as a courtesy and never as evidence, and §4.5 treats a carrier that has received only `unavailable` exactly as it treats a silent one. Appendix B's bullet says it is worth less than `ok` and why.

THE DRAFT POST, for the Zulip stream, in decision 1's framing. Register would need raising for the list.

  I am adding a keepalive to mimid for carriers that stay open
  between a client and its provider, and I would rather share the
  design and the constants than invent them privately.

  MIMI defines no liveness primitive. I checked protocol-07,
  content-10, arch-03, room-policy-04 and mls-extensions-11: no ping,
  no pong, no keepalive, no heartbeat, no liveness in any of them.
  That is right for request/response HTTPS, where the status code is
  the signal. It leaves anything holding a connection open to pick
  its own numbers, and mimid now has four such constants, each marked
  in its source as invented.

  Two things look worth agreeing on rather than each of us choosing.

  First, which component answers a probe. An answer from the socket
  layer or a timer says the socket is turning, which is the failure
  the probe exists to detect. We hit this: our IRC front end answered
  from the task that owned the connection, so it reported a healthy
  socket while the component that serves requests was blocked for
  minutes, and the client found out when its own request timed out.

  Second, how the interval is set. A responder states the longest
  idle it tolerates and the shortest probe it will answer, and the
  prober picks inside that. No defaults anywhere, because a default
  is how one codebase ends up with four invented constants.

  I have this written up as a draft if anyone wants to read it. I am
  more interested in whether other implementations are hitting the
  same thing, and what numbers you picked.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY LEAVES OUT. No mention of JMAP, per AGENTS.md; the carrier is described, never named. No scope argument, per decision 2; the post does not ask whether this is in MIMI's scope. No claim of conformance to any MIMI document. No request for permission: mimid is implementing a keepalive either way, and the question is whether the shape and the constants should be shared.
